stem: A prompt change shipped by one engineer caused hours of wrong answers before it was rolled back. The team is writing a postmortem. Which approach follows SRE postmortem practice?

choices.text: Name the engineer who shipped the change so it's clear who needs retraining
choices.reason: Blameless postmortems identify contributing causes without indicting any individual or team.

choices.text: Skip it: the problem is fixed, so a write-up now would only be a formality
choices.reason: Without a formal process for learning from incidents, they may recur; a postmortem isn't a formality.

choices.text: Focus on contributing causes and preventive actions, without blaming anyone
choices.reason: Correct: postmortems document the incident and root causes and put preventive actions in place, blamelessly.

choices.text: Record only the timeline; root causes and follow-ups go in a separate review
choices.reason: A postmortem records the incident, its impact, actions taken, root causes and follow-up actions to prevent recurrence.

takeaway: Postmortems are **blameless**: fix the systems and processes, not people, and record preventive actions.
explanation: SRE postmortems are **blameless**: they document the incident, its impact, actions taken and root causes, then put preventive actions in place, without indicting any individual or team. Option C captures that. Option A is the tempting instinct after one person's change caused the outage, but naming someone for retraining is exactly the blame the practice avoids. Skipping it (B) means incidents may recur without a learning process, and D leaves out the root causes and follow-ups a postmortem must record.

stem: Your summarization service's dashboard counts only HTTP 5xx responses and shows a 0% error rate, yet users report confidently wrong summaries. How does SRE monitoring guidance treat this?

choices.text: As latency: slow responses are the most likely cause of the bad summaries
choices.reason: Latency is the time to service a request; nothing here is slow, and wrong content is a kind of error.

choices.text: As errors: a 200 with wrong content is an implicit failure, caught by end-to-end tests
choices.reason: Correct: errors include implicit failures such as a 200 with wrong content; only end-to-end tests detect wrong content.

choices.text: As saturation: the service is too full to produce good output for every request
choices.reason: Saturation measures how "full" the service is, emphasizing its most constrained resources, not output correctness.

choices.text: Not as errors at all, because only explicit failures such as HTTP 500s count as errors
choices.reason: The errors signal also covers implicit failures and failures by policy, not only explicit ones like HTTP 500s.

takeaway: For LLM apps, a **200 with wrong content is still an error**: status codes alone miss it, so add end-to-end checks.
explanation: In SRE monitoring, the errors signal covers more than explicit failures like HTTP 500s; it also includes **implicit failures**, such as a 200 response with wrong content. A dashboard counting only 5xx responses shows 0% while summaries are wrong, and only end-to-end tests detect wrong content. Option D is the tempting trap because it matches how the dashboard counts errors today, but it ignores implicit failures. Nothing in the stem is slow, so latency (A) doesn't fit, and saturation (C) measures how full the service is, not correctness.

stem: Your team runs `claude-code-action` to review pull requests and answer `@claude` requests. Reviewers want Claude to apply the team's code style and review criteria on every run. Where does the GitHub Actions guide say to define them?

choices.text: Restated in full in each `@claude` comment whenever someone asks for a review
choices.reason: The guide says to define standards once in a repo-root `CLAUDE.md`; specific requests help, but they don't replace shared standards.

choices.text: In the repository secrets, next to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, so the workflow loads them
choices.reason: Repository secrets hold credentials such as the API key or OAuth token, not review guidelines.

choices.text: In a `CLAUDE.md` file at the repository root
choices.reason: Correct: the guide says to define code style, review criteria and project rules in a repo-root `CLAUDE.md`, which Claude follows.

choices.text: In `claude_args` as `--max-turns`, so each review stays within the standards
choices.reason: `--max-turns` limits the number of conversation turns to cap cost; it carries no style or review rules.

takeaway: Put code style, review criteria and project rules in a repo-root **CLAUDE.md**; Claude reads it on every run, so keep it concise.
explanation: The guide's best practice is to **define project standards in CLAUDE.md** at the repository root: code style, review criteria and project rules, which Claude follows when creating PRs and responding to requests. Option A is tempting because specific requests do help, but restating standards in every comment is error-prone. Secrets (B) hold credentials, and `--max-turns` (D) only caps iterations.

stem: You want `claude-code-action` to triage every newly opened issue automatically, without anyone writing `@claude`. What makes the action run without a mention?

choices.text: Remove the `prompt` input so Claude reacts to every issue event
choices.reason: With no `prompt`, the action runs in interactive mode and waits for the trigger phrase, `@claude` by default.

choices.text: Set `--max-turns` in `claude_args` so Claude acts without waiting
choices.reason: `--max-turns` limits the number of conversation turns; it has nothing to do with what starts a run.

choices.text: Provide a `prompt` input in the workflow for the issue event
choices.reason: Correct: a `prompt` input puts the action in automation mode, so Claude runs without waiting for a mention.

choices.text: Rerun `/install-github-app` and add the quick-setup review workflow
choices.reason: The review workflow reviews pull requests; issue triage without a mention needs a workflow with a `prompt` input.

takeaway: No `prompt` input = interactive mode (waits for `@claude`); a `prompt` input = automation mode (runs on the event).
explanation: `claude-code-action` has two modes: with no `prompt` input it runs in **interactive** mode and waits for the trigger phrase, `@claude` by default; with a `prompt` input it runs in **automation** mode on the event itself. To triage every new issue without a mention, the issue workflow needs a `prompt`. Option A is the tempting reversal, since removing the prompt is exactly what makes the action wait for a mention. `--max-turns` (B) only limits turns, and the quick-setup review workflow (D) reviews pull requests, not issues.

stem: Your `claude-code-action` runs use more Actions minutes and API tokens than budgeted, and some jobs run far too long. Which two changes from the GitHub Actions guide cap how much work each run can do?

choices.text: Set `--max-turns` in `claude_args` to limit iterations
choices.reason: Correct: the guide lists `--max-turns` as a way to cap how many iterations a run can take.

choices.text: Expand `CLAUDE.md` so Claude never needs to ask questions
choices.reason: The guide says to keep `CLAUDE.md` concise, since Claude reads it on every run.

choices.text: Pass `github_token` to avoid API billing on every run
choices.reason: `github_token` is for GitHub operations. It's an OAuth token, not this, that moves runs onto subscription billing.

choices.text: Set workflow-level timeouts to stop runaway jobs early
choices.reason: Correct: the guide recommends workflow-level timeouts to avoid runaway jobs.

choices.text: Check out full git history so each run starts with context
choices.reason: Not one of the guide's levers, which are specific requests, issue templates, a concise CLAUDE.md, `--max-turns`, timeouts and concurrency.

takeaway: Cap Claude in CI with `--max-turns` and workflow timeouts; keep requests specific and `CLAUDE.md` concise.
explanation: The question asks what **caps the work each run can do**, so look for hard limits rather than general hygiene. `--max-turns` (A) caps how many iterations Claude takes, and a workflow-level timeout (D) stops a runaway job outright. Option B is the trap: the guide says to keep `CLAUDE.md` concise, since Claude reads it on every run. `github_token` (C) is for GitHub operations, not billing, and full git history (E) is not one of the guide's levers.

stem: You ask Claude Code to modernize a large legacy `utils.js` that other modules depend on. Which approach matches the refactoring recipe in the Claude Code docs?

choices.text: Refactor in small, testable increments that keep behavior, then run the tests
choices.reason: Correct: the recipe asks for changes that maintain the same behavior, in small, testable increments, verified by tests.

choices.text: Skip the tests, since a behavior-preserving refactor cannot change any results
choices.reason: The recipe's last step is to verify the refactoring by running tests for the refactored code.

choices.text: Rewrite the whole file in one pass, then fix whatever the test suite reports
choices.reason: The recipe advises doing refactoring in small, testable increments, not one big rewrite.

choices.text: Drop backward compatibility so Claude can use the newest language features
choices.reason: The tips say to request that changes maintain backward compatibility when needed.

takeaway: Refactor in **small, testable increments** that preserve behavior, then have Claude run the tests to verify the refactor.
explanation: The refactoring recipe has two parts: keep the same behavior while changing code in **small, testable increments**, then verify by running tests. Because other modules depend on `utils.js`, every step needs to be checkable. Option C is tempting since tests run at the end anyway, but one big rewrite is exactly what the recipe avoids. Option B skips the verification step the recipe ends with, and D contradicts the tip to keep backward compatibility when needed.

stem: You want one Claude Code session to fix a bug in one terminal while another builds a feature in a second terminal, in the same repository, without their edits colliding. What does the Common workflows guide recommend?

choices.text: Give each session its own git worktree: a separate checkout on its own branch
choices.reason: Correct: each git worktree is a separate checkout on its own branch, so parallel sessions' edits don't collide.

choices.text: Run both sessions in the main checkout and have each one commit as it goes
choices.reason: Two sessions editing one checkout is exactly the collision worktrees avoid; each worktree is a separate checkout.

choices.text: Run `/clear` in each session so the two can't overwrite each other's edits
choices.reason: `/clear` resets a session's conversation context; it doesn't isolate files on disk.

choices.text: Turn on plan mode in one session so that only the other session writes files
choices.reason: Plan mode makes no edits until you approve its plan, so the two tasks would no longer run in parallel.

takeaway: For parallel Claude Code sessions in one repo, use **git worktrees**: each is a separate checkout on its own branch.
explanation: The guide's recipe for parallel sessions is **worktrees**: each git worktree is a separate checkout on its own branch, so one session's edits never land in the other's files. Option B is the tempting shortcut, but two sessions editing one checkout is the collision the stem wants to avoid. `/clear` (C) only resets context, and plan mode (D) blocks edits rather than isolating them.

stem: Claude just implemented a rate limiter in your session. You want a review that isn't biased toward the code Claude just wrote. What does the Claude Code best-practices guide suggest?

choices.text: Have a second session with fresh context review it, then pass its findings back
choices.reason: Correct: a fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote (the Writer/Reviewer pattern).

choices.text: Ask the same session to review its own diff carefully before it commits anything
choices.reason: The same session carries the reasoning that produced the code; the guide uses a separate session for an unbiased review.

choices.text: Run `/compact` first so the session forgets the details of how it wrote the code
choices.reason: The guide's answer to reviewer bias is a separate session with fresh context, not summarizing the current one.

choices.text: Raise the effort level for the current session so its self-review is stricter
choices.reason: The bias comes from reviewing code it just wrote; the guide fixes that with a fresh-context reviewer, not more effort.

takeaway: Review AI-written code in a **fresh context** (Writer/Reviewer), so the reviewer isn't biased toward its own work.
explanation: The bias here comes from the reviewer having **just written the code**, so the fix is a reviewer that never saw that reasoning: the Writer/Reviewer pattern, a second session with fresh context whose findings you pass back. Option B is the obvious trap, since the same session still carries the reasoning that produced the code. Summarizing with `/compact` (C) or raising effort (D) changes neither who is reviewing nor the context it reviews from.

stem: You will migrate 2,000 files from Python 2 to Python 3 by looping `claude -p` over a file list, unattended. Which two steps does the Claude Code best-practices guide recommend?

choices.text: Run every file through one interactive session so context carries across files
choices.reason: For large migrations the guide distributes work across many parallel Claude invocations, not one long session.

choices.text: Try the loop on 2–3 files first and refine the prompt before running the full set
choices.reason: Correct: refine your prompt based on what goes wrong with the first 2–3 files, then run on all of them.

choices.text: Let one prompt find and migrate all files at once instead of keeping a file list
choices.reason: The guide has Claude write the list of files to migrate to a file so the loop can read it.

choices.text: Leave tools unapproved so each invocation pauses for you to confirm every edit
choices.reason: An unattended run can't stop for approvals; the guide pre-approves tools and uses `dontAsk` to deny anything else.

choices.reason: Correct: changes made through Bash commands aren't captured by checkpoints, which aren't a replacement for git.

choices.reason: The page says to catch the SDK's typed classes rather than string-matching error messages.

choices.reason: Catching everything as one type throws away the distinctions; the page says to handle the most specific classes first.

choices.text: Catch typed classes such as `anthropic.NotFoundError`, most specific first
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK raises typed exceptions; catch those classes, most specific first, instead of string-matching messages.

choices.text: Read the raw JSON body from each failed call and branch on its message field
choices.reason: The SDK raises typed exceptions instead of returning raw JSON, and messages aren't what you should match on.

takeaway: Handle API errors by **exception class**, most specific first, never by matching message strings.
explanation: The bug is matching on **message text**, which can change, as the SDK update showed. The SDK raises typed exceptions, so catch classes such as `anthropic.NotFoundError`, handling the most specific first. Option A is tempting because it seems more precise, but it is still string-matching the message. choices.reason: Every error body includes `type` and `message`, for 4xx and 5xx alike.

Under the versioning policy, values in these error objects may expand, so new `type` values can appear and must be handled with a fallback. Option A is tempting, but the API always returns JSON errors with a top-level `error` object containing `type` and `message`, for 4xx and 5xx alike, so B is wrong too. The values are fixed machine strings like `not_found_error`, not localized (C).

stem: Your client's request to an order service times out, and you can't tell whether the server processed it. Going by HTTP method semantics, which request is safe to send again as-is?

choices.text: `POST /orders` with the same body, since an identical body makes POST idempotent
choices.reason: POST isn't guaranteed to be idempotent: calling `POST /add_row` several times adds several rows.

choices.text: `PATCH /orders/42` adding an item, since PATCH and PUT share the same guarantees
choices.reason: PATCH isn't guaranteed to be idempotent; safe methods such as GET are, as are PUT and DELETE.

choices.text: Any method at all, provided the server returned the same status code each time
choices.reason: Idempotency is about the intended effect on the server; responses can differ, e.g. DELETE returns 200 then 404.

choices.text: `PUT /orders/42` with the full order, since PUT is an idempotent method
choices.reason: Correct: PUT is idempotent, so a client can safely retry it when unsure whether the request reached the server.

takeaway: Retry blindly only **idempotent** methods (GET, PUT, DELETE…); POST and PATCH aren't guaranteed to be idempotent.
explanation: When you can't tell whether the server processed a request, only an **idempotent** method is safe to send again. PUT is idempotent, and sending the full order to `/orders/42` gives the same intended effect however many times it lands. Option A is the trap: an identical body doesn't make POST idempotent, since repeated POSTs can add repeated rows. PATCH (B) isn't guaranteed idempotent, and idempotency is about the effect on the server, not matching status codes (C).

stem: A client wants to change only a user's `status` field and sends just that field, leaving the rest of the record untouched. Which HTTP method matches these semantics?

choices.text: PATCH, which applies partial modifications to a resource
choices.reason: Correct: PATCH applies partial modifications; it is a set of instructions for modifying a resource.

choices.text: PUT, which applies the named changes and keeps other fields
choices.reason: PUT represents a complete replacement of the resource, not a partial change.

choices.text: OPTIONS, which servers use to apply small field-level edits
choices.reason: OPTIONS doesn't edit data; the page mentions it only as the request whose response may list PATCH media types in `Accept-Patch`.

choices.text: Any method, since CRUD updates map one-to-one onto HTTP
choices.reason: HTTP is different from CRUD, and the two should not be confused.

takeaway: **PATCH** = partial change (not guaranteed idempotent); **PUT** = full replacement (idempotent).
explanation: The deciding detail is that the client sends **only the field it wants changed** and the rest must stay untouched. That is PATCH, which applies partial modifications to a resource. Option B is the trap: PUT sounds like 'update', but it represents a **complete replacement** of the resource, not a partial change. OPTIONS (C) doesn't edit data, and D wrongly treats HTTP as a one-to-one map of CRUD.

stem: Your service emits JSON that several partner systems parse with different JSON libraries. Which two practices does RFC 8259 say keep that JSON interoperable?

choices.text: Keep every name within each object unique
choices.reason: Correct: when names are unique, all receiving implementations agree on the name-value mappings.

choices.text: Start each networked JSON text with a byte order mark
choices.reason: Implementations MUST NOT add a byte order mark to the beginning of a network-transmitted JSON text.

choices.text: Repeat a key to override it, since parsers keep the last
choices.reason: With duplicate names, behavior is unpredictable: many keep the last pair, others error or report all pairs.

choices.text: Don't let consumers depend on object member order
choices.reason: Correct: parsers differ on exposing member order; implementations that don't depend on it are interoperable.

choices.text: Encode the text as UTF-16 for wider Unicode coverage
choices.reason: JSON exchanged between systems outside a closed ecosystem MUST be encoded using UTF-8.

takeaway: Interoperable JSON: unique names, no reliance on member order, UTF-8 with no BOM.
explanation: Interoperability means every receiver, whatever library it uses, agrees on the data. **Unique names** (A) make all implementations agree on the name-value mappings, and **not depending on member order** (D) avoids a point where parsers differ. Option C is the tempting one, but with duplicate names behavior is unpredictable: many parsers keep the last pair, others error or report all pairs. A BOM (B) is forbidden on networked JSON, and text exchanged between open systems must be UTF-8, not UTF-16 (E).

stem: Your asyncio app fans out 500 `AsyncAnthropic` calls, and you want at most 10 of them in flight at once. Which standard-library primitive fits?

choices.text: An `asyncio.Lock()`, which lets up to 10 tasks hold it at the same time
choices.reason: A Lock is a mutex: it guarantees exclusive access, so only one task holds it at a time.

choices.text: An `asyncio.Event()`, set once 10 tasks have started running
choices.reason: An Event notifies multiple tasks that something happened via a flag; it doesn't count holders.

choices.text: A `threading.Semaphore(10)`, since asyncio primitives are thread-safe
choices.reason: asyncio's primitives are documented as not thread-safe; for tasks on one event loop, use `asyncio.Semaphore`.

choices.text: An `asyncio.Semaphore(10)`, entered with `async with` per call
choices.reason: Correct: acquire() blocks when the counter is zero, so `Semaphore(10)` caps concurrent holders at 10; `async with` is preferred.

takeaway: Cap async concurrency with **`asyncio.Semaphore(n)`** and `async with` around each call.
explanation: You need a **counter of concurrent holders**: `asyncio.Semaphore(10)` blocks `acquire()` when the counter hits zero, so at most 10 calls are in flight, and `async with` around each call is the preferred form. Option A is the trap: a Lock is a mutex, so only one task holds it at a time, not ten. An Event (B) is a flag that notifies tasks, not a counter, and `threading.Semaphore` (C) is wrong for tasks on one event loop.

stem: You run 50 summaries with `asyncio.gather(*tasks)`. One call raises an exception. You want every other result **plus** the failures, matched to their inputs. What should you change?

choices.text: Nothing: by default `gather()` cancels the rest and returns partial results
choices.reason: By default the first exception propagates immediately; the other awaitables aren't cancelled and keep running.

choices.text: Pass `return_exceptions=True`, so failures come back in the result list
choices.reason: Correct: exceptions are then treated like results and aggregated, in the same order as the awaitables you passed.

choices.text: Pass `return_exceptions=True` and re-sort the results by completion time
choices.reason: No re-sort is needed: the order of result values corresponds to the order of the awaitables.

choices.text: Catch the exception and call `cancel()` on the gather to collect the rest
choices.reason: Catching the propagated exception loses the result list, and cancelling the gather afterwards won't cancel the other awaitables.

takeaway: `gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` returns results and exceptions together, in input order.
explanation: By default, the first exception from `gather()` propagates immediately, so you lose the result list. With `return_exceptions=True`, exceptions are treated like results and aggregated, in the **same order as the awaitables** you passed, which gives you both successes and failures matched to inputs. Option C is tempting but adds an unneeded step, since order already follows the inputs. Option A misstates the default: the others aren't cancelled and no partial list comes back.

stem: A faulty commit from last week is on the team's main branch, with later commits on top. You want to undo only its changes and keep a record that you did. Which git command fits?

choices.text: `git reset --hard`, which throws away just that one commit's patch
choices.reason: Git points to `reset --hard` for throwing away uncommitted changes, not for reversing one earlier commit.

choices.text: `git restore --source`, which deletes the commit from the history
choices.reason: `git restore --source` extracts specific files as they were in another commit; it doesn't remove commits.

choices.text: `git revert <commit>`, recording a new commit that reverses it
choices.reason: Correct: git revert records new commits that reverse the effect of earlier commits, often a single faulty one.

choices.text: `git revert` with uncommitted edits, so they fold into the reversal
choices.reason: git revert requires a clean working tree, with no modifications from the HEAD commit.

takeaway: Use **`git revert`** to undo a past commit by recording a new, reversing commit; it needs a clean working tree.
explanation: Two constraints matter: undo **only one past commit** with later commits on top, and **keep a record** of doing it. `git revert <commit>` records a new commit that reverses the earlier one, so history stays intact. Option D is tempting because it also uses revert, but revert requires a clean working tree, so uncommitted edits can't fold in. `reset --hard` (A) throws away uncommitted changes, and `restore --source` (B) extracts files rather than removing commits.

stem: You spent an hour in Claude Code debugging the auth flow. Now you want to start an unrelated CSS cleanup in the same session, and Claude keeps bringing up auth files. What does Anthropic's Claude Code best-practices guide recommend?

choices.reason: Compaction keeps a summary of the auth work in context; the guide's fix for switching to unrelated work is `/clear`, which resets the context entirely.

choices.text: Run `/clear` to reset the context before starting the CSS work

choices.text: Add a line to CLAUDE.md telling Claude to ignore the earlier auth discussion

choices.reason: The guide warns that irrelevant context in long sessions can reduce performance and sometimes distract Claude; its fix for this is `/clear`.

explanation: The new task is **unrelated**, and old auth context is distracting Claude. The guide says to use `/clear` between unrelated tasks, which resets the context so nothing from the auth work is carried over. Option A is the trap: `/compact` keeps a summary of the auth work in context, which is the very thing you want gone. A CLAUDE.md note (C) loads every session and should hold only broad guidance, and D is wrong because irrelevant context in long sessions can reduce performance.

stem: You've corrected Claude Code three times on the same bug, and each attempt is still wrong in a new way. The session is long and full of failed fixes. What does Anthropic's best-practices guide suggest?

choices.text: Send a fourth correction in capital letters so Claude weighs it above the rest
choices.reason: Each correction adds to a context already polluted with failed approaches; louder wording doesn't remove them.

choices.text: Press `Esc` to stop Claude and keep redirecting it from the current context
choices.reason: `Esc` stops Claude with context preserved, so the failed approaches stay in the conversation; it's for correcting early, not resetting.

choices.text: Run `/clear` and start over with a sharper prompt that uses what you learned
choices.reason: Correct: after two failed corrections, `/clear` and write a better initial prompt; a clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms one full of corrections.

choices.text: Add each failed approach to CLAUDE.md so future sessions avoid repeating it
choices.reason: If CLAUDE.md gets too long, Claude ignores half of it because rules get lost in the noise; the fix here is a fresh session.

takeaway: Corrected twice and still wrong? **Start fresh** with a better prompt; accumulated failed attempts pollute the context.
explanation: The guide's rule of thumb: after **two failed corrections**, run `/clear` and write a better initial prompt using what you learned, because a clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms one full of corrections. Three failed fixes in a long session means the context is polluted with failed approaches. Option B is tempting since `Esc` lets you redirect, but it preserves context, so the failures stay. Louder wording (A) and stuffing CLAUDE.md (D) don't remove the clutter.

stem: Your Claude Code session is getting long, and the next phase builds on the API changes made so far. You want to free up context but make sure what remains keeps the API details. Which command fits?

choices.text: `/clear`, then describe the API changes again by hand
choices.reason: `/clear` starts fresh with an empty context, so the details you wanted kept are gone from it.

explanation: You want two things: **free up context** and **keep the API details**. `/compact` replaces the history with a summary, and adding instructions such as `Focus on the API changes` tells that summary what to keep. Option B is tempting because it frees the most space, but `/clear` empties the context, so the details are gone and you'd retype them by hand. `/context` (C) only shows what's using context, and `/rename` (D) just names the session.

stem: Early in a Claude Code session you told Claude in chat to always use `pnpm`, never `npm`. After the session compacts, Claude starts running `npm` again. What's the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Repeat the rule in chat marked IMPORTANT, so the summary keeps it

choices.text: Put it in a rule file with `paths:` scoped to `package.json`

choices.text: Put it in a CLAUDE.md inside a subdirectory such as `scripts/`

explanation: Instructions given only in chat can disappear after compaction. The **project-root CLAUDE.md** is different: after `/compact`, Claude re-reads it from disk and re-injects it, so a rule there survives. Options B and C are the subtle traps: path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md files load on demand, so after compaction the rule may be missing until a matching file is touched. Marking a chat message IMPORTANT (A) doesn't make it persist.

stem: Yesterday you named a Claude Code session `oauth-migration` with `/rename`, then worked in two other sessions in the same repo. Which commands take you straight back into `oauth-migration`?

choices.text: `claude --continue`
choices.reason: It reopens the most recent session in the current directory, which is now one of the other two.

choices.text: `claude --resume oauth-migration` from your shell
choices.reason: Correct: `claude --resume <name>` resumes the named session directly.

choices.text: `claude -n oauth-migration`
choices.reason: `-n` sets the name of a new session at startup; it doesn't resume the old one.

choices.text: `/resume oauth-migration` inside a running session
choices.reason: Correct: `/resume <name>` switches to the named session from inside an active session.

explanation: The session has a name from `/rename`, so you can resume it **by name**: `claude --resume oauth-migration` from the shell (B), or `/resume oauth-migration` inside a running session (D). Option A is the trap: `--continue` reopens the **most recent** session in the directory, and the stem says you worked in two others since. `-n` (C) names a new session, and `/clear` with a name (E) names the session you're leaving and starts fresh.

stem: A developer's Claude Code sessions slow down and drift as they fill with file reads, side questions and old tasks. Which two habits does Anthropic's best-practices guide recommend for keeping the main context clean?

choices.text: Run `/clear` whenever you switch to an unrelated task
choices.reason: Correct: `/clear` between unrelated tasks resets the context window entirely.

choices.text: Add every correction you make to CLAUDE.md so nothing is ever lost
choices.reason: Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions; keep it to what applies broadly.

choices.text: Ask Claude to investigate the whole codebase before scoping the task
choices.reason: Unscoped investigation is a named failure pattern: Claude reads hundreds of files and fills the context.

choices.text: Delegate research to subagents, which report back summaries
choices.reason: Correct: subagents explore in separate context windows and report back summaries, keeping your main conversation clean.

choices.text: Keep correcting in the same session until Claude gets it right
choices.reason: Repeated corrections pollute the context with failed approaches; after two, `/clear` and write a better prompt.

takeaway: Keep the main context lean: **`/clear`** between tasks and send exploration to **subagents**.
explanation: Both correct habits keep unneeded material out of the main context. `/clear` between unrelated tasks (A) resets the window, and delegating research to subagents (D) keeps exploration in separate context windows that report back summaries. Option C is tempting because more investigation feels thorough, but unscoped investigation is a named failure pattern that fills the context. Bloating CLAUDE.md (B) makes Claude ignore instructions, and repeated corrections (E) pollute context.

stem: A prompt prototyped in claude.ai correctly mentions today's date in its answers. The same prompt sent through the Claude API, with no system prompt, gets the date wrong or omits it. What explains the difference?

The stem's detail, an API call with **no system prompt**, means nothing gives the model the date. Option A is tempting because it blames the model, but the difference is the system prompt, not training. Nothing is stripped by the API (C), and memory (D) isn't where the date comes from.

stem: A CI script runs Claude Code on every pull request. The team wants a few review rules delivered at the system-prompt level rather than as CLAUDE.md content, which reaches Claude as a user message after the system prompt. What does the memory guide recommend?

To deliver instructions at the system-prompt level, the guide recommends `--append-system-prompt`, which is passed at launch and suits a CI script. Option B is the trap: an IMPORTANT heading changes emphasis, not delivery, so it's still a user message. An `@path` import (C) is still CLAUDE.md content, and auto memory (D) loads as context like CLAUDE.md.

stem: Your multi-tenant app stores customer documents with the Files API. To pick a document, the browser sends a `file_id` that your server passes straight into the Messages request. What does the Files API guide warn about?

choices.text: Nothing: a `file_id` only works with the API key that uploaded the file
choices.reason: Files are scoped to the workspace: any API key with access to that workspace can access any file uploaded there.

choices.text: Set `expires_in_seconds` on uploads so stale IDs from users stop working
choices.reason: Expiration is a lifecycle feature, not an access control; it doesn't stop one user from sending another user's live file ID.

choices.text: Treat file IDs as server-side references and isolate tenants by workspace
choices.reason: Correct: never accept file IDs from users, since one could read another's upload; map users to files in your app and use a workspace per tenant.

choices.text: Files are scoped to the conversation that uploaded them, so cross-user reads fail
choices.reason: Uploaded files aren't scoped to an end user, conversation or session; any request in the same workspace can reference them.

takeaway: File IDs are **workspace-wide**: keep them server-side, never take them from users, and give each tenant its own workspace.
explanation: Files are **scoped to the workspace**, not to an end user, conversation or API key, so any request in that workspace can reference any file. If the browser supplies the `file_id`, one user could send another's ID and read their upload. Keep IDs server-side, map users to files in your app, and give each tenant its own workspace. Option D is the trap because it assumes per-conversation scoping. Expiration (B) is lifecycle, not access control, and A is false too.

stem: A HIPAA-covered app uses structured outputs. To stop Claude inventing names, a developer puts each patient's name into an `enum` in the JSON schema. What does the structured-outputs guide say?

choices.text: Fine: structured outputs are HIPAA eligible, so the schema is protected too
choices.reason: Eligibility doesn't extend to schemas: compiled schemas are cached separately and don't get the PHI protections that prompts and responses do.

choices.text: Fine, as long as the names go into a `pattern` regex instead of an `enum`
choices.reason: PHI must not appear in `pattern` regular expressions either, nor in property names or `const` values.

choices.text: Don't: keep PHI out of schemas and send it only in message content
choices.reason: Correct: schemas are cached separately without PHI safeguards, so PHI belongs only in message content (prompts and responses).

choices.text: Fine, because schemas are discarded as soon as the response returns
choices.reason: The JSON schema is temporarily cached for up to 24 hours since last use; it's prompts and responses that aren't retained.

takeaway: Never put PHI in a **schema** (property names, `enum`, `const`, `pattern`): schemas are cached apart from protected message content.
explanation: Structured outputs being HIPAA eligible covers **prompts and responses**, not schemas. Compiled schemas are cached separately, for up to 24 hours since last use, without the PHI protections that message content gets. So patient names belong only in message content, never in an `enum`. Option A is the trap: eligibility doesn't extend to the schema. Moving names to a `pattern` (B) is still the schema, and D is wrong because schemas are cached, not discarded.

stem: Your agent's tools include `create_pr`, `review_pr`, `merge_pr`, `list_issues` and `send_message`, spanning GitHub and Slack, and Claude sometimes picks the wrong one. Which two changes does the Define tools guide recommend?

choices.text: Shorten each description to one line to save prompt tokens
choices.reason: Detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance; aim for at least 3–4 sentences each.

choices.text: Merge the PR operations into one tool with an `action` parameter
choices.reason: Correct: grouping `create_pr`, `review_pr` and `merge_pr` into one tool with an `action` parameter reduces selection ambiguity.

choices.text: Prefix names with their service, like `github_list_prs` and `slack_send_message`
choices.reason: Correct: namespacing names by service makes tool selection unambiguous as your library grows.

choices.text: Return each record in full, with internal references, so Claude has all context
choices.reason: Return only high-signal fields and stable, semantic IDs; bloated responses waste context and bury what matters.

choices.text: Add a parameter asking Claude to explain its step-by-step reasoning per call
choices.reason: A parameter asking for step-by-step reasoning may lead to a `reasoning_extraction` refusal; ask for a short explanation instead.

takeaway: Make tool choice easy: **consolidate** related actions into one tool and **namespace** tool names by service.
explanation: The symptom is Claude **picking the wrong tool**, so the fixes reduce selection ambiguity. Grouping `create_pr`, `review_pr` and `merge_pr` into one tool with an `action` parameter (B) removes near-duplicates, and namespacing by service (C), such as `github_` and `slack_`, makes each name unambiguous. Option A is the tempting trap: detailed descriptions are the most important factor in tool performance, so shortening them hurts. Bloated responses (D) and step-by-step reasoning parameters (E) are discouraged.

stem: An agent must call your booking tools with valid parameters and then finish with a JSON report your code parses. A teammate says you'll need two separate requests for that. What's correct?

choices.text: Right: JSON outputs and strict tool use can't appear in one request
choices.reason: The guide lists combined usage as compatible: both features can be used together in the same request.

choices.text: Use citations for the report, since they work with JSON outputs
choices.reason: Citations are incompatible with JSON outputs; the API returns a 400 if citations are enabled with `output_config.format`.

choices.text: Prefill `{` for the report and skip `output_config.format`
choices.reason: Message prefilling is incompatible with JSON outputs; the guide's way to get both is JSON outputs plus strict tool use in one request.

choices.text: Use `strict: true` tools and `output_config.format` together
choices.reason: Correct: combined, Claude calls tools with guaranteed-valid parameters and returns structured JSON, which suits agentic workflows.

takeaway: JSON outputs (what Claude **says**) and strict tool use (how it **calls tools**) work together in one request.
explanation: JSON outputs control **what Claude says** and strict tool use controls **how it calls tools**, and the guide lists them as compatible in one request. With `strict: true` tools plus `output_config.format`, Claude calls tools with guaranteed-valid parameters and returns structured JSON, which suits agentic workflows. Option A is the teammate's mistaken claim. Citations (B) and prefilling (C) are each incompatible with JSON outputs, so neither delivers the report.

stem: You want a code-review plugin for yourself in one client repository only, without affecting teammates or your other projects. Which install scope fits, and where is it recorded?

choices.text: User scope, recorded in `~/.claude/settings.json`
choices.reason: User scope enables the plugin for you in every project on this machine.

choices.text: Local scope, recorded in `.claude/settings.local.json`
choices.reason: Correct: local scope enables the plugin for you in this repository only, with the entry in `.claude/settings.local.json`.

choices.text: Project scope, recorded in `.claude/settings.json`
choices.reason: Project scope writes to the committed `.claude/settings.json` and enables the plugin for everyone in the repository.

choices.text: Managed scope, recorded in your organization's managed settings
choices.reason: Managed-scope plugins are installed by your organization through managed settings, and you can't enable, disable or uninstall them in `/plugin`.

takeaway: Plugin scopes: **user** = all your projects, **project** = everyone in the repo, **local** = just you in this repo.
explanation: Match the scope to who should get the plugin: **just you, in this repo only**. That's local scope, recorded in `.claude/settings.local.json`. Option C is the trap, since it is also per-repo, but project scope writes to the committed `.claude/settings.json` and enables it for everyone in the repository. User scope (A) applies to every project on your machine, and managed scope (D) is set by your organization.

stem: A CI job runs `claude -p "/plugin install formatter@your-org"` before its review step, and Claude replies that `/plugin` isn't available in this environment. How should the job install the plugin?

choices.text: Add `--verbose` so the `-p` run can open the `/plugin` panel
choices.reason: `/plugin` doesn't run in `claude -p` and other non-interactive runs; plugins are managed there with `claude plugin` commands.

choices.text: Run `claude plugin install formatter@your-org` from the shell first
choices.reason: Correct: install from your shell with `claude plugin` commands; plugins you've already installed do load in `-p` runs.

choices.text: Run `/reload-plugins` in the `-p` prompt before `/plugin install`
choices.reason: The blocker is `/plugin` itself, which doesn't run in `claude -p`; installing from the shell avoids it.

choices.text: Plugins never load in `-p` runs, so move the review to an interactive session
choices.reason: Plugins you already installed do load in `-p` runs; only the `/plugin` command is unavailable there.

takeaway: In `claude -p`, **`/plugin` doesn't run**: install with `claude plugin install` from the shell, and installed plugins still load.
explanation: In `claude -p` and other non-interactive runs, the **`/plugin` command doesn't run**; plugins are managed with `claude plugin` commands from the shell, and installed plugins do load in `-p` runs. So the CI job should run `claude plugin install formatter@your-org` first. Option D is the trap, overcorrecting by moving to an interactive session, when only `/plugin` is unavailable. `--verbose` (A) and `/reload-plugins` (C) don't make `/plugin` work.

stem: A bank uses Claude in Amazon Bedrock. Compliance now requires that inference for one product stay in a single AWS region. The rest of its traffic has no residency rule and should be as cheap and available as possible. How should it route requests?

choices.text: Send all traffic to the global endpoint, which keeps each request in its home region
choices.reason: Global endpoints use dynamic routing across all available regions, so they can't guarantee single-region processing.

choices.text: Use regional endpoints for all traffic, since they cost the same as global ones
choices.reason: Regional endpoints carry a 10% pricing premium over global endpoints, so using them everywhere adds cost for traffic with no residency rule.

choices.text: Regional endpoint for the regulated product, global endpoint for everything else
choices.reason: Correct: a regional endpoint resolves to the region you specify, for data residency, at a 10% premium; the global endpoint has no premium and routes for availability.

choices.text: Use the global endpoint with an inference profile that limits it to one region
choices.reason: Inference profiles route across multiple regions within a geography such as US or EU, which doesn't meet a single-region requirement.

takeaway: On Bedrock, **global** endpoints route dynamically with no premium; **regional** endpoints pin one region for residency at a 10% premium.
explanation: Two requirements pull in different directions: one product needs **single-region** processing, the rest wants **cheapest and most available**. A regional endpoint pins the region you specify, at a 10% premium, while the global endpoint routes dynamically with no premium. So split the traffic. Option A is the trap: global routing spans regions and can't guarantee residency. All-regional (B) adds needless cost, and inference profiles (D) still span a geography, not one region.

stem: In Microsoft Foundry you deployed Claude Opus 5.5 under the custom deployment name `support-opus`. Requests that send `"model": "claude-opus-5-5"` to your resource's endpoint fail with a deployment-not-found error. What should `model` contain?

choices.text: `support-opus`, the deployment name you chose in the Foundry portal
choices.reason: Correct: the deployment name becomes the value you pass in `model`. It defaults to the model ID, but a custom name like `support-opus` replaces it.

choices.text: `anthropic.claude-opus-5-5`, the provider-prefixed ID cloud platforms use
choices.reason: Foundry doesn't take a provider-prefixed ID: the deployment name becomes the `model` value, and the default name is the plain model ID.

choices.text: The Target URI shown on the Details tab of the deployment
choices.reason: The Target URI is your endpoint URL; the `model` parameter should contain your deployment name.

choices.text: `claude-opus-5-5@foundry`, the model ID plus a platform suffix
choices.reason: Foundry uses no such suffix: the deployment name you choose becomes the value you pass in `model`.

takeaway: On Foundry, `model` is your **deployment name**, which matches the model ID only if you kept the default name.
explanation: On Foundry, the **deployment name** becomes the value you pass in `model`. It defaults to the model ID, which is why `claude-opus-5-5` would work only with the default name; here you chose `support-opus`, so that's what `model` needs. Option B is tempting because provider-prefixed IDs feel platform-correct, but Foundry doesn't use one. The Target URI (C) is the endpoint URL, and no `@foundry` suffix exists (D).

stem: You estimate cost for a PDF Q&A feature by counting only the tokens in each PDF's extracted text. Actual input usage comes out noticeably higher. Why?

choices.text: PDF input carries a separate per-page fee on top of normal token prices
choices.reason: Standard API pricing applies with no additional PDF fees; the extra tokens come from each page's image.

choices.text: Each page is also converted to an image, which adds image tokens per page
choices.reason: Correct: each page is sent as extracted text plus an image, and the image is costed like any other image input.

choices.text: The extracted text is tokenized at a higher rate than plain text input
choices.reason: Text token costs use standard API pricing; the difference is the image each page is converted into.

choices.text: Token counting can't estimate PDFs, so usage always differs from estimates
choices.reason: The guide recommends the token counting API to estimate costs for your specific PDFs.

takeaway: A PDF page costs its **text tokens plus image tokens**; use token counting to estimate real documents.
explanation: Each PDF page is sent as **extracted text plus an image**, and that image is costed like any other image input. Counting only the text misses the image tokens, so real usage comes out higher. Option A is tempting because it also explains extra cost, but standard pricing applies with no additional PDF fees. Text isn't priced at a special rate (C), and the guide actually recommends the token counting API to estimate PDFs (D).

stem: Your RAG app retrieves help-center articles and passes them to Claude as plain text. Users want every claim in an answer to show which article supports it, with that article's title and URL, without special prompting. What fits best?

choices.text: Ask Claude in the prompt to add a source URL after every sentence it writes
choices.reason: Search result blocks give native citations that carry the source and title you provided, with no special prompting needed.

choices.text: Send each article as a `search_result` block with citations enabled
choices.reason: Correct: search result blocks let Claude cite your content like web search results, each citation carrying your source and title.

choices.text: Put all the articles in the system prompt so Claude treats them as trusted
choices.reason: Where the text sits doesn't create citations; Claude cites search results automatically when citations are enabled on them.

choices.text: Return the articles from a tool, since only tool results can carry citations
choices.reason: Search results can come from tool calls or be passed directly as top-level content in user messages.

takeaway: For RAG answers with source attribution, pass retrieved content as **`search_result` blocks** with citations enabled.
explanation: **Search result blocks** exist for RAG source attribution: each citation carries the source and title you provided, and Claude cites them automatically when citations are enabled. Option A is tempting, but it relies on prompting instead of the native feature, which needs no special prompting. The system prompt (C) doesn't create citations, and D is wrong because search results can also be passed directly in user messages.

stem: Your raw SSE parser receives `text_delta` events with `index: 0` and `input_json_delta` events with `index: 1` in the same stream. How should it assemble the final message?

choices.text: Concatenate every delta's text in arrival order into one reply string
choices.reason: Deltas update different blocks: `input_json_delta` holds partial JSON for a `tool_use` input, not text to append to the reply.

choices.text: Apply each delta to the content block at its `index` in the final `content` array
choices.reason: Correct: each content block has an `index` matching its position in the final Message `content` array, and a delta updates the block at that index.

choices.text: Treat `index` as a retry counter and keep only the deltas that carry the highest index
choices.reason: `index` identifies a content block, not a retry; both blocks belong in the final message.

choices.text: Ignore `index: 1`, since a stream only ever carries one content block
choices.reason: A stream carries a series of content blocks, each with its own `content_block_start`, deltas and `content_block_stop`.

takeaway: Streamed deltas are **per content block**: route each one by its `index`, which matches the final `content` array.
explanation: A stream carries a **series of content blocks**, and each block's `index` matches its position in the final `content` array. The `text_delta` events build block 0, while the `input_json_delta` events build block 1, partial JSON for a `tool_use` input. Option A is the trap: concatenating everything would splice tool-input JSON into the reply text. `index` isn't a retry counter (C), and streams aren't limited to one block (D).

stem: Your app sends `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: 10000}` with Claude Sonnet 4.6. After you switch the model to Claude Opus 5.5, every request fails with a 400 error. What change does the extended thinking guide describe?

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` well above `budget_tokens` so the budget has room to fit
choices.reason: Newer models reject `type: "enabled"` itself, whatever the budget and `max_tokens` values are.

choices.text: Switch to `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` and set depth with `effort`
choices.reason: Correct: remove `budget_tokens`, set `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` and control reasoning depth with `output_config.effort`.

choices.text: Move `budget_tokens` into `output_config`, where newer models read it
choices.reason: The migration removes `budget_tokens` entirely; `output_config` takes `effort`, not a token budget.

choices.text: Stay on Claude Sonnet 4.6, where `budget_tokens` is the long-term setting
choices.reason: `budget_tokens` is deprecated on the 4.6 models, so staying only postpones the same migration.

takeaway: Newer models reject manual `budget_tokens` thinking: switch to **adaptive thinking** and steer depth with `effort`.
explanation: Manual extended thinking is deprecated on the 4.6 models and **rejected** by Claude 4.7 and later, including Claude Opus 5.5. The migration is to remove `budget_tokens`, set `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` and control depth with `effort`. Option C is the tempting half-step, but `output_config` takes `effort`, not a budget. Raising `max_tokens` (A) can't fix a rejected mode, and staying on 4.6 (D) only delays it.

stem: A Message Batch has ended, and its `request_counts` show 9,600 `succeeded`, 150 `errored` and 250 `expired`. Which two follow-up actions are sound?

choices.text: Resubmit the 250 expired requests in a new batch; they weren't billed
choices.reason: Correct: expired requests hit the 24-hour expiration before reaching the model, and you aren't billed for them.

choices.text: Read each errored result's `result.error`; fix invalid requests before retrying
choices.reason: Correct: errored results carry the standard error shape, and possible errors include invalid requests as well as internal server errors.

choices.text: Match results to inputs by line number, since results come back in request order
choices.reason: Result order is not guaranteed; match each result to its request by `custom_id`.

choices.text: Expect a charge for the 150 errored requests at the batch discount
choices.reason: You are not billed for errored requests, nor for canceled or expired ones.

choices.text: Download all results within 24 hours of the batch ending, or they're deleted
choices.reason: Batch results are available for 29 days after the batch is created.

takeaway: Errored, canceled and expired batch requests **aren't billed**: resubmit expired ones, and fix errored ones using `result.error`.
explanation: Errored, canceled and expired requests **aren't billed**, so act on each type. Expired requests hit the 24-hour expiration before reaching the model, so resubmitting them in a new batch is sound (A). Errored results carry the standard error shape in `result.error`, and some are invalid requests that must be fixed before retrying (B). Option C is the tempting trap: result order isn't guaranteed, so match by `custom_id`. Errored requests aren't charged (D), and results last 29 days (E).

stem: Every request in a large Message Batch shares the same 50k-token system prompt, but the results show few cache reads. What does the batch guide recommend to raise the cache hit rate?

choices.text: Use identical `cache_control` blocks on the shared prompt in every request
choices.reason: Correct: include identical `cache_control` blocks in every request; hits are best-effort (typically 30% to 98%) because requests run concurrently.

choices.text: Enable `stream: true` so each request reuses the previous request's cache
choices.reason: `stream: true` isn't supported in batch requests; including it returns a validation error.

choices.text: Set `max_tokens: 0` on a first batch request to pre-warm the cache
choices.reason: `max_tokens: 0` isn't supported in a batch: an entry written during batch processing would likely expire before the follow-up runs.

choices.text: Do nothing: batches always hit the cache because requests run in order
choices.reason: Batch requests are processed asynchronously and concurrently, so cache hits are only best-effort.

takeaway: Caching and batch discounts **stack**, but hits are best-effort: put identical `cache_control` blocks in every batched request.
explanation: Batch requests run **asynchronously and concurrently**, so cache hits are best-effort (typically 30% to 98%). To raise the hit rate, put **identical `cache_control` blocks** on the shared prompt in every request. Option D is the trap: it assumes requests run in order and always hit, which they don't. `stream: true` (B) isn't supported in batches, and a `max_tokens: 0` pre-warm (C) isn't supported either.

stem: You're rolling out Claude Code to 300 engineers through Amazon Bedrock. Everyone should be on the same Opus version, and you want to choose when they move to a new one. What does the model configuration guide recommend?

choices.text: Keep the `opus` alias, which uses the newest Opus on every provider
choices.reason: Aliases point to a recommended version for each provider and update over time; on Bedrock that default can lag the newest release.

choices.text: Set `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL` to a version-specific Bedrock model ID
choices.reason: Correct: on third-party providers, pin model versions before rollout by setting the model env vars to specific IDs; this controls when users move.

choices.text: Have each engineer pick Opus with `/model` and save it as their default
choices.reason: `/model` saves one person's default; pinning the env vars to specific version IDs is how the guide says to control when users move.

choices.text: Set `"model": "opus"` in each repository's shared `.claude/settings.json`
choices.reason: That still uses the alias, which updates over time; pinning needs a version-specific model ID.

takeaway: On Bedrock, Google Cloud or Foundry, **pin** with `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL` set to version IDs before rollout.
explanation: Two goals: **everyone on the same version** and **you choose when they move**. On third-party providers, the guide says to pin before rollout by setting the model env vars, such as `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL`, to version-specific IDs. Option A is the trap: aliases update over time, and on Bedrock the default can lag the newest release. `/model` (C) only sets one person's default, and `"model": "opus"` (D) still follows the alias.

stem: A team's shared `.claude/settings.json` sets `"model": "opus"`. Their eval results shifted after a Claude Code update started resolving `opus` to a newer Opus release. How do they keep the model fixed until they choose to move?

choices.text: Set `model` to a full model name such as `claude-opus-5-5`
choices.reason: Correct: aliases point to the recommended version and update over time; to pin a version, use the full model name.

choices.text: Set `model` to `opusplan` so Opus stays fixed during planning
choices.reason: `opusplan` uses `opus` in plan mode and `sonnet` for execution, so it still follows the aliases.

choices.text: Set `model` to `default` to lock in the version used today
choices.reason: `default` clears any model override and reverts to your account's runtime default; it doesn't pin a version.

choices.text: Set `model` to `opus[1m]` for a version that never changes
choices.reason: `opus[1m]` adds a 1M-token context window to the `opus` alias; it still follows the alias.

takeaway: Aliases like `opus` **move** to newer releases over time; pin a full model name for reproducible results.
explanation: Aliases such as `opus` **point to the recommended version and update over time**, which is exactly what shifted the evals. To keep the model fixed until you choose to move, set `model` to a full name such as `claude-opus-5-5`. Option D is tempting because it looks more specific, but `opus[1m]` only adds a 1M-token window to the alias and still follows it. `opusplan` (B) also follows aliases, and `default` (C) clears the override rather than pinning.

stem: Security has approved only Sonnet models for Claude Code across the company. Engineers must not be able to switch to Opus with `/model`, `--model` or `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`. Which configuration enforces this?

choices.text: An `availableModels` allowlist of Sonnet models in managed settings
choices.reason: Correct: a managed `availableModels` allowlist applies to `/model`, `--model`, `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` and the `model` setting, and users can't extend it.

choices.text: `"model": "sonnet"` in each project's committed `.claude/settings.json`
choices.reason: The `model` setting is an initial selection, not enforcement; `/model`, `--model` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` can still select Opus.

choices.text: A CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude never to switch away from Sonnet
choices.reason: Instructions to Claude don't control which model a user selects; an allowlist in managed settings does.

choices.text: `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL` set in every engineer's shell profile
choices.reason: That only changes what the `sonnet` alias resolves to; it doesn't stop anyone selecting Opus.

takeaway: To **restrict** models org-wide, use an `availableModels` allowlist in managed settings; a `model` setting is only a starting choice.
explanation: This needs **enforcement**, not a default. An `availableModels` allowlist in managed settings applies everywhere a user can pick a model, including `/model`, `--model` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, and user, project or local settings can't extend it. Option B is tempting, but the `model` setting is only an initial selection that those overrides can change. A CLAUDE.md rule (C) instructs Claude, not model selection, and D only changes what `sonnet` resolves to.

stem: Your plugin calls an MCP tool from the `secrets-vault` plugin, declared as the bare dependency `"secrets-vault"`. A new `secrets-vault` release renamed that tool, and your plugin broke for every user who updated. How do you prevent a repeat?

choices.text: Ask users to turn off auto-update for every marketplace they use
choices.reason: Without a constraint, the dependency moves to each new release whenever users update, manually or automatically.

choices.text: Declare it as an object with a tested range such as `"version": "~2.1.0"`
choices.reason: Correct: for a git-backed dependency, `~2.1.0` keeps users on `2.1.x` patches and never moves them to `2.2`; widen the range after you test a newer release.

choices.text: Add `secrets-vault` to `allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn`
choices.reason: That allowlist governs dependencies from another marketplace; it doesn't constrain versions.

choices.text: List the dependency twice so both versions install side by side
choices.reason: A dependency resolves to one version that satisfies every installed plugin's range; versions aren't installed side by side.

takeaway: Unconstrained plugin dependencies track the **latest** release; pin a tested semver range in `plugin.json` `dependencies`.
explanation: A bare dependency like `"secrets-vault"` has **no version constraint**, so it moves to each new release whenever users update. Declare it as an object with a tested range: for a git-backed dependency, `~2.1.0` keeps users on `2.1.x` patches and never moves them to `2.2`; widen it after testing. Option A is tempting, but the dependency moves on manual updates too, not just automatic ones. C governs cross-marketplace dependencies, and versions aren't installed side by side (D).

stem: Your security team needs Claude Code permission rules that developers can't override from any of their own settings files or launch flags. Which two delivery mechanisms fit?

choices.text: Server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console
choices.reason: Correct: server-managed settings are a managed source; nothing a developer puts in their own files changes them.

choices.text: A `managed-settings.json` file or MDM policy deployed to each machine
choices.reason: Correct: MDM or OS-level policies and `managed-settings.json` files are managed sources, which nothing in a developer's own files changes.

choices.text: A committed `.claude/settings.json` in every repository
choices.reason: Shared project settings are files in each developer's clone, and their own `.claude/settings.local.json` is applied over them.

choices.text: The `--settings` flag in a wrapper script everyone launches with
choices.reason: `--settings` applies above user, project and local files but below managed settings, and a developer can launch without it.

choices.text: Each developer's own `~/.claude/settings.json`, written once by a setup script
choices.reason: User settings are the developer's own file, which they can edit; it's for personal preferences.

takeaway: Policy developers can't override belongs in **managed settings**: server-managed from the admin console, or a managed file or MDM policy.
explanation: Developers can't override **managed** sources, because nothing in their own files changes them. Server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console (A) and a `managed-settings.json` file or MDM policy on each machine (B) are both managed. Option D is the tempting trap: `--settings` ranks above user, project and local files, but below managed settings, and a developer can simply launch without it. Project files (C) are overridden by local settings, and user settings (E) are the developer's own.

stem: Your root CLAUDE.md has grown to 600 lines and adherence is dropping. Much of it is API-handler conventions that only matter under `src/api/`, plus a 40-step release procedure. Which two changes cut what loads into every session?

choices.text: Move the API conventions to a `.claude/rules/` file scoped by `paths`
choices.reason: Correct: path-scoped rules load only when Claude works with matching files, which reduces noise and saves context space.

choices.text: Move the 40-step release procedure out of CLAUDE.md into a skill

stem: A teammate expects that moving your Go service from raw HTTP calls to Anthropic's Go SDK will also give you an agent loop that runs your tools for you. What does the SDKs overview page say the client SDKs are?

choices.text: General-purpose Messages API clients: you still send each request yourself
choices.reason: Correct: the client SDKs are general-purpose Messages API clients; with them you send each request and handle each response.

choices.text: Agent runtimes that provide the agent loop and run your tools automatically
choices.reason: That's Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK and Claude Managed Agents, which work at a higher level and provide the agent loop and tool execution.

choices.text: Python and TypeScript wrappers only, so Go services must stay on raw HTTP
choices.reason: Client SDKs exist for seven languages: Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby.

choices.text: Compatibility layers that expose Claude through another framework's API
choices.reason: That describes libraries and integrations such as OpenAI SDK compatibility, which are not general-purpose Messages API clients.

takeaway: A client SDK wraps the **Messages API**; the agent loop comes from the Agent SDK, Claude Code or Managed Agents.
explanation: The SDKs page separates three layers: client SDKs (general-purpose Messages API clients), libraries that expose Claude through another framework, and higher-level agent products. The Go SDK is a client SDK, so you still send each request and handle each response (A). Option B is the tempting confusion of "SDK" with the Claude Agent SDK, which is what provides the agent loop. C is wrong because Go has an official SDK, and D describes libraries and integrations.

stem: Users of your chat app stare at an empty reply area until Claude Opus 5.5's whole answer arrives, and then it appears all at once. Total generation time is acceptable. What does Anthropic's latency guide recommend to make the app feel faster?

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` so the full answer can be delivered sooner
choices.reason: `max_tokens` is a hard limit on the response's length; it doesn't make the answer arrive any sooner.

choices.text: Lower `temperature` to 0.2 for shorter, more focused replies
choices.reason: Claude 4.7 and later models accept only the default `temperature` and return a 400 error for any other value.

choices.text: Ask for an exact word count so that every reply is shorter
choices.reason: The guide says word-count limits work less well than paragraph or sentence limits, and shorter replies still appear only when complete.

choices.text: Stream the response and render the text as it arrives
choices.reason: Correct: streaming lets the model start sending its response before the output is complete, which significantly improves perceived responsiveness.

takeaway: When a user is waiting, **stream**: text that appears as it's generated makes the app feel faster.
explanation: The stem's key detail is that total time is fine; the problem is the blank wait before anything appears. Streaming sends the response before it's complete, so users see output in real time, which the guide says significantly improves perceived responsiveness (D). Option B is tempting from older advice, but Claude 4.7 and later models reject non-default `temperature`. Raising `max_tokens` (A) doesn't speed delivery, and word counts (C) still leave the reply arriving all at once.

stem: You're sorting workloads into the Message Batches API or real-time Messages calls. Which two are good fits for the Message Batches API?

choices.text: A large-scale evaluation that runs thousands of test cases
choices.reason: Correct: the batch guide lists large-scale evaluations, processing thousands of test cases efficiently, among its use cases.

choices.text: A live chat reply that a customer is waiting on right now
choices.reason: Batches suit tasks that don't need immediate responses; most finish in under 1 hour, which is far too slow for a waiting customer.

choices.text: A support UI that renders tokens as they're generated
choices.reason: `stream: true` isn't supported in batch requests: batch results come back as a single file, not a stream.

choices.text: A moderation backlog of user posts that can wait a few hours
choices.reason: Correct: content moderation of large volumes of user-generated content is a listed batch use case, and nothing here needs an immediate response.

choices.text: A coding tool that sends `speed: "fast"` for low latency
choices.reason: Fast mode isn't supported in batches: it tunes synchronous latency, which doesn't apply to asynchronous batch processing.

takeaway: Batch work **nobody is waiting on**: evals, moderation, analysis and bulk generation, at 50% of the price.
explanation: The deciding question is whether anyone is waiting. Batches are processed asynchronously at half price, with most finishing in under an hour, so they fit bulk work such as large-scale evaluations (A) and a moderation backlog that can wait (D). Option B is the tempting cost-saving idea, but a waiting customer needs a real-time reply. Streaming (C) and fast mode (E) are both rejected inside batch requests.

stem: Users wait on each reply from your web backend, which awaits `AsyncAnthropic` calls. A teammate suggests moving these calls to the Message Batches API to save money. Why is that a poor fit?

choices.text: Batch requests are billed above standard Messages prices, so costs would rise
choices.reason: Batch usage is charged at 50% of standard API prices, so the price part of the claim is right.

choices.text: Batches can't carry system prompts or multi-turn history, so chats would break
choices.reason: System messages and multi-turn conversations can both be included in a batch.

choices.text: Batches stream each result back as soon as it finishes, so nothing changes
choices.reason: `stream: true` isn't supported in batches; results are available once all requests complete or after 24 hours.

choices.text: Batch results are fetched later by polling, so users would wait far too long
choices.reason: Correct: a batch is processed asynchronously and you poll for results; most batches finish in under 1 hour, which suits work that doesn't need an immediate response.

takeaway: Batches suit work nobody is waiting on; a user waiting for a reply needs a normal (or streamed) Messages call.
explanation: The Message Batches API processes requests in the background and you poll for results, with most batches finishing in under an hour (D). That suits bulk work, not users waiting on replies. Batches really do cost 50% less (so A is wrong), and B and C misstate what batches support.
